title: Is AI Against God’s Will?
paragraphs: Is AI Against God’s Will?

The Bible never mentions artificial intelligence by name. But it says far more about AI than many Christians realize—because the deepest question was never whether a machine can think. The deepest question is whether the human heart will still bow.
Your phone lights up in the dark.
You cannot sleep.
So you reach for it.
A few taps, a few words, and suddenly something answers you.
It can explain a difficult passage. Write a letter. Generate an image. Translate a language. Help organize a business. Produce a song. Imitate a voice. Summarize thousands of words in seconds.
And somewhere beneath the fascination, a question begins whispering.
Should Christians even be doing this?
Maybe you have wondered whether artificial intelligence is something believers should reject.
Maybe you have heard someone call AI demonic.
Maybe another Christian told you it is simply another tool.
Maybe you have watched technology advance so quickly that something inside you feels uneasy.
And perhaps the question haunting you is not technological at all.
Perhaps it is spiritual.
Is AI against God's will?
Here is where we need to be careful.
The Bible does not say, “Thou shalt not use artificial intelligence.”

Artificial intelligence as we know it did not exist in the biblical world. So anyone claiming that Scripture explicitly identifies modern AI as inherently sinful is claiming more than the text itself says.
But that does not mean Scripture leaves Christians without an answer.
The Bible gives us something better than a verse containing the letters “A.I.”
It gives us a theology of creation.
A theology of humanity.
A theology of tools.
A theology of wisdom.
A theology of idolatry.
A theology of truth.
And above everything else, it gives us Jesus Christ.
So before asking whether a machine is becoming too human, Scripture forces us to confront something much more uncomfortable:
What are humans becoming while using the machine?
Go back to the beginning.
Before computers.
Before electricity.
Before cities.
Before the first hammer struck metal.
Before humanity built anything at all.
There was God.
And then came this staggering declaration in Genesis 1:27:
וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha'adam betzalmo, betzelem Elohim bara oto.
“And God created humankind in His image; in the image of God He created him.”
At the heart of that Hebrew sentence stands the expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — betzelem Elohim — “in the image of God.”
That distinction matters enormously.
A machine may imitate human language.
It may recognize patterns.
It may produce something astonishingly beautiful.
It may simulate conversation so effectively that you momentarily forget you are interacting with software.
But Scripture does not say that human beings possess dignity because we process information quickly.
Our worth does not come from computational ability.
We bear the image of God.
AI does not suddenly become an image-bearer merely because its output resembles something an image-bearer might say.
And that means Christians should resist two opposite errors.
We should not worship AI.
And we should not automatically demonize AI.
We should judge what we do with it beneath the authority of God.
Because humanity has always made tools.

The Bible itself describes human beings developing instruments, agriculture, craftsmanship, construction, writing, ships, weapons, musical instruments, architecture, roads, systems of commerce and countless other applications of human creativity.
And tools are capable of being directed toward radically different ends.
Wood can become a table where hungry people are fed.
Wood can become an idol before which people kneel.
Stone can become part of a temple.
Stone can become something thrown in hatred.
Words can comfort someone contemplating despair.
Words can destroy someone's reputation through a lie.
Technology magnifies human capacity.
But increased capacity does not automatically produce increased holiness.
That is where the AI conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps the greatest spiritual danger of artificial intelligence is not that someday a machine will pretend to be God.
Perhaps the more immediate danger is that we will use the machine while pretending that we are.
We want unlimited knowledge.
Immediate answers.
Instant creation.
Frictionless productivity.
Recognition without years of formation.
Influence without character.
Results without patience.
Answers without prayer.
And suddenly the story becomes very old.
Older than Silicon Valley.
Older than computers.
Older than civilization.
“Did God really say...?”
The serpent's temptation in Eden was not fundamentally about fruit.
It was about autonomy.
“You will be like God.”
That temptation never disappeared.
Human beings simply keep building more sophisticated places to hide it.
So the Christian question about AI cannot merely be, “What can this technology do?”
It must also be:
“What is this technology teaching my heart to desire?”
That question can hurt.
Because AI may reveal something we would rather not admit.
Maybe you do not merely want help writing.
Maybe you want praise for something you did not actually labor to understand.
Maybe you do not merely want efficiency.
Maybe you are becoming addicted to avoiding difficulty.
Maybe you do not merely want information about Scripture.
Maybe you are beginning to substitute generated answers for actually sitting before God with an open Bible.
Maybe you are asking a machine questions you have stopped bringing to God in prayer.
That does not automatically make the machine sinful.
It exposes the heart.
And Scripture has always been relentless about the heart.
Paul gives us a principle in 1 Corinthians 10:31 that reaches far beyond food and drink:
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”
Whatever you do.
That includes what you search.
What you generate.
What you publish.
What you imitate.
What you automate.
What you create.
What you pretend you created.
What you watch.
What you allow technology to do to another human being.
And what you do with AI when nobody else knows.
The question therefore changes.
Not merely:
“Can a Christian use AI?”
But:
“Can I use this particular application of AI in this particular way for the glory of God?”
That is a much harder question.
Because sometimes the answer will be yes.
Sometimes it will be no.
And sometimes wisdom will tell you that although something may technically be permissible, you should walk away from it.
Imagine using AI to help translate educational material for people who otherwise could not access it.
Imagine helping someone with limited literacy communicate more clearly.
Imagine accelerating research while carefully verifying the sources.
Imagine assisting a small ministry overwhelmed by administrative work so human beings have more time to care for actual people.
Imagine using technology to make Scripture study resources more accessible while still pointing people back to Scripture itself.
There is nothing inherently ungodly about those purposes.
But now turn the mirror.
Imagine using AI to fabricate evidence against someone.
To impersonate a person.
To manufacture pornography.
To deceive customers.
To plagiarize.
To create false testimonies.
To manufacture a sermon that a pastor has neither studied nor spiritually wrestled with, then present it as the fruit of his own prayer and labor.
To flood the internet with misinformation because clicks matter more than truth.
To manipulate lonely people.
To replace compassion with automation simply because loving someone personally is inconvenient.
Same broad technological category.
Different heart.
Different purpose.
Different moral reality.
Scripture's concern with truth alone should make Christians extraordinarily cautious here.
Jesus calls Satan “the father of lies” in John 8:44.
God does not need deception to accomplish His purposes.

So when AI is used to manufacture lies, fake identities, false accusations, dishonest academic work, fraudulent images, counterfeit evidence, or deliberately misleading spiritual content, the Christian cannot hide behind the sentence, “It's only a tool.”
A hammer may be only a tool.
But if I deliberately strike my neighbor with it, my moral responsibility does not disappear because the hammer lacked intentions.
Neither does yours.
And there is another boundary Christians desperately need to recover.
AI can provide information about God. It cannot become God.
It can generate words about prayer.
It cannot hear your prayer as your Father.
It can summarize doctrines about forgiveness.
It cannot forgive your sins.
It can produce a paragraph about loneliness.
It cannot enter covenant relationship with you.
It can analyze biblical language.
It cannot become the Holy Spirit.
It can imitate pastoral language.
It cannot replace the Body of Christ.
It can describe Jesus.
It cannot save you.
That last distinction is everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity climbing toward God through intelligence.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
John opens his Gospel with words infinitely greater than anything a machine could claim:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος — En archē ēn ho Logos.
“In the beginning was the Word.”
Not an algorithm.
Not human ingenuity.
Not accumulated information.
The Word.
And John continues:
καὶ ὁ Λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος.
“The Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
Then comes the breathtaking declaration of John 1:14:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο — Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Christianity does not proclaim that information became salvation.
It proclaims that the eternal Son entered human history.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus wept.
Jesus ate with sinners.
Jesus confronted hypocrisy.
Jesus welcomed the broken.
Jesus carried a cross.
Jesus shed real blood.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose.
No technological revolution can improve upon Calvary.
No artificial intelligence can rewrite the Gospel.
And no machine can bear the weight of your sin.
Only Christ did that.
This is why the question “Is AI against God's will?” eventually becomes too small.
The deeper question is:
Is your life surrendered to God's will?
Because you can reject every AI program on earth and still worship yourself.
You can throw away your smartphone and remain proud.
You can refuse every algorithm and still lie.
You can live without artificial intelligence and still live without Jesus.
The enemy does not need advanced technology to destroy a person.
Sin has been doing that since Genesis.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Our greatest crisis therefore is not artificial intelligence.
It is human rebellion against a holy God.
And our greatest hope is not better technology.
It is Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why this subject unsettles us so deeply.
We are frightened that machines might expose what humanity really is.
But the cross already did.
At Calvary we see what human sin is capable of.
The innocent Son of God rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And yet at that same cross we see something else.
Grace.
The scandal of grace.
The place where human evil meets divine mercy.
The place where judgment and forgiveness meet.
The place where sinners discover that their story does not have to end with what they have done.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by flattering us into believing we are basically fine.
He rewrites everything through repentance, forgiveness, redemption and new life.
That means perhaps you came into this article expecting a verdict on technology.
Instead, Scripture has brought the verdict closer.
To you.
To me.
To the secret places.
What controls you?
What do you trust?
Where do you run first when you are afraid?
What are you willing to compromise to get ahead?
Are you becoming more truthful as technology becomes more powerful?
More loving?
More discerning?
More dependent upon Christ?
Or simply more efficient at hiding?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Maybe your problem is not AI at all.
Maybe there is something else you have allowed to sit where only Jesus belongs.
Approval.
Money.
Pornography.
Achievement.
Politics.
Ministry.
Knowledge.
Your phone.
Your audience.
Your own intelligence.
Even your reputation as a “good Christian.”
Anything can become an idol when we demand from it what belongs to God.
And the answer to idolatry is not merely deleting an application.
It is repentance.
It is returning.
It is surrender.
It is looking again toward Christ.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become testimony.

Let someone scrolling through them discover that Christians are not people pretending to have no struggles. We are people learning, repenting, stumbling, rising, confessing and returning again and again to Christ.
And send this article to someone who is wrestling with AI.
Both of them may need the same reminder:
The machine is not Lord. Jesus is.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry helps proclaim biblical truth, sharing it can help place that truth in front of someone who might never otherwise encounter it. Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully and for God's glory—not through guilt, pressure or an attempt to purchase favor from God.
And there is something else we want believers to know about.
Because AI will change.
Technology will change.
The arguments will change.
The headlines will change.
But you will need this truth again:
Christ does not surrender His throne every time humanity invents something powerful.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting God Himself.
God is not impoverished without us.
We need His grace.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
So use technology if you can use it faithfully.
Reject it where it requires compromise.
Question it when it asks for too much trust.
Verify what it tells you.
Never surrender your conscience to it.
Never let convenience replace compassion.
Never let generated words replace genuine prayer.
Never let artificial intelligence become artificial discipleship.
And never mistake access to endless information for intimacy with God.
You can have the world's knowledge in your pocket and still have an empty soul.
You can ask a machine ten thousand questions about Jesus...
and still never answer the question Jesus asks you:
“Who do you say that I am?”
That is the question no algorithm can answer for you.
One day your devices will go silent.
Your accounts will disappear.
Your achievements will belong to history.
The technologies that seem revolutionary today will become museum pieces tomorrow.
But Christ will still be King.
So perhaps the question you should carry away from this article is no longer:
“Is AI against God's will?”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, is there anything in me that is against Yours?”
Because the greatest danger was never that a machine might become your master.
It was that your heart might forget it already has one.
